content: Globally, approximately 38.3 million people are living with HIV, according to UNAIDS data from 2013. In 2013 alone, 3 million new HIV infections were reported. This highlights the urgent need for additional safe and effective HIV prevention strategies. Men who have sex with men (MSM) bear a disproportionate burden of HIV in most countries, even in regions with generalized HIV epidemics. Although there are effective HIV prevention interventions for MSM, access to these services is often hindered by political and structural barriers, as well as the stigma and marginalization faced by this population. The high prevalence of HIV among MSM suggests that current prevention methods are inadequate, and new prevention modalities are necessary. The safety of the drugs used for PrEP, specifically tenofovir and emtricitabine, has been established through their use in treatment and safety trials involving uninfected individuals. Over the past decade, five clinical trials (Phase IIb and Phase III) have evaluated the effectiveness of PrEP among various populations, including people who inject drugs, serodiscordant couples, heterosexual women, and high-risk MSM. One notable Phase III trial, the iPrEx study, specifically examined the efficacy of a daily combination of tenofovir and emtricitabine in preventing HIV among MSM. Conducted across six countries on four continents, this trial demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV transmission in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Adherence to the recommended regimen was a critical factor, with efficacy increasing to 73% among participants who reported taking the medication on 90% or more of days. Drug resistance was rare, occurring only in two participants who had undetected acute HIV infection at baseline. The study also reported few safety concerns and observed a trend toward risk reduction, including increased condom use and fewer sexual partners. In 2012, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines recommending PrEP for serodiscordant couples, MSM, and transgender individuals at high risk of HIV. These guidelines were informed by systematic reviews, including updates to the evidence base for PrEP among MSM. The updated review focused on oral PrEP containing tenofovir and included randomized controlled trials evaluating its use among MSM. The review also incorporated data on key outcomes such as HIV infection rates, adverse events, condom use, and the number of sexual partners. The systematic review identified 764 citations and 139 conference abstracts, ultimately including four studies reported in five articles. These studies varied in purpose, drug regimens, and sample sizes. The primary Phase III efficacy trial, iPrEx, was highlighted for its robust design and high-quality evidence. Additional findings from smaller studies supported the safety and feasibility of PrEP among MSM. The iPrEx trial, conducted among 2,499 participants in six countries, demonstrated a 44% reduction in HIV risk with daily oral PrEP. Adverse events were similar between the PrEP and placebo groups, and no significant differences in condom use or the number of sexual partners were observed. Other studies, such as Project PrEPare and the CDC safety study, reported similar findings, with no major differences in adverse events or risk compensation behaviors. Awareness and willingness to use PrEP among MSM have increased since the release of the iPrEx results, but global awareness remains limited. Willingness to use PrEP varies widely, with most studies reporting acceptance rates between 40% and 70%. Barriers to PrEP use include concerns about effectiveness, side effects, cost, accessibility, and stigma. Facilitators include perceived benefits, convenience, and support from healthcare providers. Healthcare providers generally support PrEP but express concerns about drug resistance, adherence, and the integration of PrEP into existing care models. Cost-effectiveness studies suggest that PrEP can be a valuable addition to HIV prevention programs, particularly in high-incidence settings.
